adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — P1 [confidence: 100] The selection rule `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` leaves the three built-in full providers tied at `return 200;`, so any classpath containing two of them silently selects one according to ServiceLoader discovery order instead of enforcing the formerly required single-provider configuration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order() = 200, meaning if multiple are on the classpath, the selection becomes non-deterministic (depends on ServiceLoader discovery order). This is a valid architectural concern - the old behavior threw an exception when multiple providers were found, enforcing explicit configuration. The new behavior silently picks one. However, this is not a bug per se - it's a design decision that changes behavior. The code works as written, but the finding raises a legitimate concern about the tie-breaking logic when multiple full providers exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:47 — [P2, confidence 75, code `AuthzClientCryptoProvider prov = new AuthzClientCryptoProvider();`] Direct construction bypasses the required `AuthzClient.create`/`CryptoIntegration.init` service-loading and priority-selection path, so a packaged-provider discovery regression ships with no acceptance coverage.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the test bypasses required initialization and thus doesn't provide proper acceptance coverage. However, the test is specifically designed to test the ECDSACryptoProvider functionality of AuthzClientCryptoProvider in isolation - it directly tests the ASN1 encoding/decoding logic. This is a valid unit test approach. The test verifies the cryptographic conversion methods work correctly, which is exactly what unit tests should do. The service-loading mechanism is tested implicitly through the META-INF/services file and would be covered by integration tests. The direct construction is intentional for unit testing the specific component.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:54 — [P2, confidence 75, code `byte[] asn1Des = prov.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rsConcat, algorithm.getSignatureLength());`] The test only feeds the emitted DER back into the same decoder instead of verifying it with an independent JCA verifier, so an externally unacceptable DER encoding ships while the round-trip assertion still passes.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java only performs a round-trip test (sign -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS) and compares the intermediate results (rsConcat vs rsConcat2). It does not verify the signature using JCA's Signature.verify() with the re-encoded DER. This means if the ASN1 encoder produces non-standard but self-consistent output, the test would pass but the signatures might not be verifiable by external systems. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added crypto code, not a bug in the production code itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — [P1][confidence:100][code:`int order();`] Adding this abstract method makes every already-compiled external `CryptoProvider` fail with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` invokes `order()` during `ServiceLoader` discovery.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `int order();` is added as a new abstract method to the `CryptoProvider` interface (line 44 in CryptoProvider.java). Java interfaces with abstract methods require all implementing classes to provide an implementation. Any external/third-party implementations of `CryptoProvider` that were compiled against the old interface version (without the `order()` method) will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` calls `order()` during the sorting operation (visible in CryptoIntegration.java: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`). This is a real binary compatibility breaking change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — [confidence=100][severity=P1][code=`.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`] when two discovered providers share the highest order, stable sorting preserves ServiceLoader's classpath-dependent order and `foundProviders.get(0)` silently starts the process with one provider instead of surfacing the conflicting runtime configuration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that when multiple CryptoProviders have the same order value, the sorting is stable and preserves ServiceLoader's classpath-dependent order. Looking at the diff, the code sorts by order in reversed order and takes foundProviders.get(0). If two providers have the same highest order (e.g., both DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider have order() returning 200), the selection becomes non-deterministic based on classpath ordering. The code only logs debug messages about which provider was selected and which were ignored, but doesn't detect or warn about this tie condition. This is a real edge case bug where runtime behavior could vary unexpectedly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — [P2, confidence 75, code `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len); System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len);`] An ES JWS whose signature is a valid fixed-length r||s value followed by arbitrary attacker-controlled bytes is verified as the unmodified signature because the conversion copies only that prefix into DER.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misunderstands the code flow. The `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` method takes a DER-encoded signature as input and converts it to concatenated R||S format - it doesn't validate signatures. The `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` method takes a concatenated R||S signature and converts to DER. The signature verification itself happens elsewhere (in Java's Signature class), not in these conversion methods. These are just format conversion utilities. The claim that 'arbitrary attacker-controlled bytes' would be verified is incorrect because: 1) The input to `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` is already a DER-encoded signature from the Signature.sign() operation, 2) The actual signature verification would happen separately using the converted format, and 3) The conversion methods don't perform verification - they just convert between formats.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — P2, confidence 100: The mirror assertion `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2);` accepts a non-JCA-compatible DER encoding whenever this provider's decoder accepts its own output, so a deployed verifier rejects signatures despite all three tests passing.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the test is flawed because it only verifies round-trip consistency (rsConcat -> asn1Der -> rsConcat2) rather than JCA compatibility. However, examining the test code, it actually starts with a real JCA signature (signature.sign() produces valid DER), converts it to concatenated RS format, then back to DER, then back to RS again. The test verifies rsConcat equals rsConcat2, which confirms the round-trip works. The original 'sign' variable is a valid JCA DER signature, so if asn1derToConcatenatedRS correctly parses it and concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces valid DER that can be parsed back, the implementation is correct. The finding's claim that 'a deployed verifier rejects signatures' is speculative and not demonstrated by the diff - the test does use real JCA signatures as input.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — P2, confidence 75: `keyPair = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair();` never selects P-384 or P-521, so the ES384 and ES512 cases can pass using default-curve coordinates padded to their larger widths while a conversion defect on real 48- or 66-byte coordinates reaches production.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test uses KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() without specifying curve parameters, which defaults to a single curve (typically P-256). The test then runs the same keyPair through ES256, ES384, and ES512 test cases. While the ASN1 encoding/decoding logic is being tested, the test doesn't actually verify the conversion works correctly with real 48-byte (P-384) or 66-byte (P-521) coordinate data. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added crypto conversion code, though it's not a bug in the production code itself.
